questiontext.text: A clause is best defined as:

answer.text: A boolean expression that contains no logical operators

feedback.text: Correct — a clause is atomic, e.g. x > 0 or a single boolean variable.

answer.text: Any boolean expression joined by &&, ||, or !

feedback.text: That describes a predicate, which is built from clauses.

answer.text: A single row of a truth table

feedback.text: A truth-table row is one assignment of values, not a clause.

answer.text: A test case that makes a predicate true

feedback.text: That is a test, not a clause.

generalfeedback.text: A clause (condition) is a boolean expression with no logical operators (&&, ||, !). Predicates are formed by connecting clauses with those operators.

questiontext.text: A predicate is:

answer.text: An expression formed from one or more clauses connected by logical operators

feedback.text: Correct — clauses joined by &&, ||, ! form a predicate.

answer.text: Always an expression with no logical operators

feedback.text: That is a clause; a predicate may contain operators.

answer.text: An arithmetic expression that returns a number

feedback.text: A predicate is boolean-valued, not numeric.

answer.text: A loop condition that must be an inequality

feedback.text: A predicate need not be an inequality nor tied to a loop.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate is a boolean expression built from clauses connected by logical operators. A single clause with no operators is itself the simplest predicate.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a single clause (not a compound predicate)?

feedback.text: Correct — a relational expression with no logical operators is one clause.
This joins two clauses with &&, so it is a predicate.
The ! operator makes this a compound predicate over the clause p.
This joins two clauses with ||, so it is a predicate.

generalfeedback.text: A clause contains no logical operators. Only x >= 5 qualifies; the others use &&, ||, or !.

questiontext.text: How many clauses does the predicate (p && q) || !r contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the clauses are p, q, and r.
There are three atomic conditions: p, q, r.
The operators &&, ||, ! are not clauses; only p, q, r are.
This is a compound predicate with three clauses, not one.

generalfeedback.text: Clauses are the atomic boolean expressions. In (p && q) || !r they are p, q, and r — three clauses.

questiontext.text: Predicate Coverage (PC) requires that:

answer.text: The predicate evaluates to both true and false at least once

feedback.text: Correct — one test making it true, one making it false.

answer.text: Each clause evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: That is Clause Coverage (CC), not PC.

answer.text: Every combination of clause values is exercised

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

answer.text: Each clause determines the predicate's value at least once

feedback.text: That is the active-clause idea (ACC), which is out of scope here.

generalfeedback.text: PC only constrains the whole predicate: it must take both truth values at least once. It says nothing about individual clauses.

questiontext.text: Clause Coverage (CC) requires that:

answer.text: Each clause evaluates to both true and false at least once

feedback.text: Correct — every atomic condition must take on both values.

answer.text: The whole predicate evaluates to both true and false

feedback.text: That is Predicate Coverage (PC).

answer.text: All 2^n combinations of clause values are exercised

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage (CoC).

answer.text: Each clause independently determines the predicate

feedback.text: That is active-clause coverage, stronger than plain CC.

generalfeedback.text: CC requires each clause to be both true and false at least once, regardless of what the enclosing predicate does.

questiontext.text: Combinatorial (Clause) Coverage (CoC) requires that:

answer.text: Every one of the 2^n truth-value combinations of the n clauses is exercised

feedback.text: Correct — the full truth table (subject to feasibility).

answer.text: The predicate takes both true and false

feedback.text: That is only Predicate Coverage (PC).

answer.text: Each clause takes both true and false

feedback.text: That is only Clause Coverage (CC).

answer.text: n + 1 carefully chosen tests are executed

feedback.text: n + 1 is the minimal size for CACC/MC-DC, which is out of scope here.

generalfeedback.text: CoC (a.k.a. ACoC) demands all 2^n combinations of the n clauses' truth values — the complete truth table.

questiontext.text: How many rows are in the full truth table of a predicate with 2 clauses?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^2 = 4.
2 is the minimum for PC or CC, not the number of rows.
8 = 2^3 would be three clauses.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate with n clauses has 2^n truth-table rows; for n = 2 that is 4.

questiontext.text: How many rows are in the full truth table of a predicate with 3 clauses?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^3 = 8.
4 = 2^2 would be two clauses.
The count is 2^3 = 8, not 3^2.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate with n clauses has 2^n rows; for n = 3 that is 8.

questiontext.text: How many rows are in the full truth table of a predicate with 4 clauses?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^4 = 16.
8 = 2^3 would be three clauses.
2^4 = 16, not 4 times 3.
32 = 2^5 would be five clauses.

generalfeedback.text: A predicate with n clauses has 2^n rows; for n = 4 that is 16.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a AND b

questiontext.text: Of the 4 truth-table rows, how many make a && b true?

feedback.text: Correct — only a=T, b=T satisfies a conjunction.
Only the all-true row satisfies a && b.
3 is the count for a || b, not a && b.
A conjunction is false whenever any clause is false.

generalfeedback.text: A conjunction is true only when every clause is true, so exactly 1 of the 4 rows satisfies a && b.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a OR b

questiontext.text: Of the 4 truth-table rows, how many make a || b true?

feedback.text: Correct — only a=F, b=F fails.
1 is the count for a && b.
Only the all-false row fails, leaving 3.
The all-false row a=F, b=F does not satisfy a || b.

generalfeedback.text: A disjunction is false only when every clause is false, so 3 of the 4 rows satisfy a || b.

name.text: Satisfying rows of (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: Of the 8 truth-table rows, how many make (a && b) || c true?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 rows with c=T, plus the one row a=T, b=T, c=F.
The 4 rows with c=T count, but a=T, b=T, c=F also satisfies it, giving 5.
Recount — exactly 5 of the 8 rows are true.
c=T alone already gives 4 true rows.

generalfeedback.text: Whenever c=T the predicate is true (4 rows); when c=F it needs a=T and b=T (1 more). Total = 5 of 8.

questiontext.text: What is the minimum number of tests needed to satisfy Predicate Coverage for a single predicate?

feedback.text: Correct — one test makes it true, one makes it false.
One test can only produce one truth value; PC needs both.
4 relates to a 2-clause truth table, not the PC minimum.

answer.text: It depends on the number of clauses

feedback.text: PC ignores clause count; 2 tests always suffice for one predicate.

generalfeedback.text: PC needs the predicate to be both true and false, so at least 2 tests, independent of how many clauses it has.

questiontext.text: A clause contains no logical operators (&&, ||, !).

feedback.text: Correct — clauses are atomic; operators combine them into predicates.
By definition a clause has no logical operators; adding one makes it a compound predicate.

generalfeedback.text: A clause is a boolean expression with no logical operators. Joining clauses with &&, ||, or ! yields a predicate.

questiontext.text: For a predicate whose clauses can be set independently, what is the minimum number of tests that satisfies Clause Coverage, regardless of the number of clauses?

feedback.text: Correct — one all-true test and one all-false test flip every clause.
Two tests suffice: set all clauses true, then all false.
n + 1 is the MC/DC minimum, not the CC minimum.
2^n is Combinatorial Coverage, far more than CC needs.

generalfeedback.text: When clauses are independent, one all-true and one all-false test give every clause both values, so CC needs only 2 tests.

questiontext.text: A predicate has 3 independent clauses. How many test requirements does Combinatorial Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^3 = 8 combinations.
3 is closer to the CC size, not every combination.
4 = n + 1 is the MC/DC minimum, not CoC.
6 falls short of the full 2^3 = 8 combinations.

generalfeedback.text: CoC requires all 2^n combinations; for n = 3 that is 8.

questiontext.text: Among PC, CC, and CoC, which statement is correct?

answer.text: CoC subsumes both PC and CC

feedback.text: Correct — exercising all combinations covers both PC and CC.
PC and CC are incomparable; neither subsumes the other.
CC does not subsume PC — see the a && b counterexample.
It is the other way around: CoC is the strongest of the three.

generalfeedback.text: A test set covering all 2^n combinations necessarily makes the predicate both true and false (PC) and each clause both values (CC), so CoC subsumes both.

questiontext.text: Which statement about Predicate Coverage and Clause Coverage is correct?

answer.text: Neither subsumes the other; they are incomparable

feedback.text: Correct — each can be met without the other.
Not so: a || b with tests {(T,F),(F,F)} meets PC but not CC.
Not so: a && b with tests {(T,F),(F,T)} meets CC but not PC.
They are distinct and incomparable, not equivalent.

generalfeedback.text: PC and CC are incomparable: there are test sets meeting one but not the other in each direction.

questiontext.text: For p = a && b, which 2-test set satisfies Clause Coverage but not Predicate Coverage? (rows given as (a, b))

feedback.text: Correct — a and b each take both values, yet p is false in both rows.
Here p is true then false, so this satisfies PC too.
b takes both values but a stays true, so CC is not met; also p is true then false.
a never becomes true, so this fails CC.

generalfeedback.text: With (T,F) and (F,T), a is {T,F} and b is {F,T} (CC met), but a && b is false both times, so PC fails.

questiontext.text: For p = a || b, which 2-test set satisfies Predicate Coverage but not Clause Coverage? (rows given as (a, b))

feedback.text: Correct — p is true then false (PC met), but b is never true, so CC fails.
Here both clauses take both values, so CC is also satisfied.
Both clauses take both values here, so CC is satisfied too.
p is true in both rows, so PC is not satisfied.

generalfeedback.text: With (T,F) and (F,F), p is true then false (PC met), but b stays false, so CC fails.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a AND (b OR c)

questiontext.text: Of the 8 truth-table rows, how many make a && (b || c) true?

feedback.text: Correct — a=T (4 rows), minus the row where b=F and c=F.
Among the 4 rows with a=T, the one with b=F, c=F fails, leaving 3.
5 is the count for (a && b) || c, a different predicate.
a must be true, so at most 4 rows qualify; the correct count is 3.

generalfeedback.text: The predicate needs a=T and (b || c). a=T gives 4 rows; removing b=F, c=F leaves 3.

name.text: Satisfying rows of (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: Of the 8 truth-table rows, how many make (a || b) && c true?

feedback.text: Correct — c must be true, and among those 4 rows only a=F, b=F fails.
c=T gives 4 rows, but a=F, b=F, c=T fails (a || b is false), leaving 3.
Recount — exactly 3 rows satisfy it.
Too few — three of the c=T rows satisfy a || b.

generalfeedback.text: c must be true (4 rows); of those, a || b holds in 3 (all but a=F, b=F). Total = 3.

name.text: Satisfying rows of NOT a OR (b AND c)

questiontext.text: Of the 8 truth-table rows, how many make !a || (b && c) true?

feedback.text: Correct — all 4 rows with a=F, plus a=T with b=T, c=T.
The 4 rows with a=F all count, and a=T, b=T, c=T adds one more, giving 5.
Recount — exactly 5 rows satisfy it.
a=F alone already yields 4 true rows.

generalfeedback.text: When a=F the predicate is true (4 rows); when a=T it needs b=T and c=T (1 row). Total = 5.

questiontext.text: Any test set that satisfies Combinatorial Coverage also satisfies Predicate Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — covering all combinations includes rows where the predicate is true and where it is false.
CoC subsumes PC: exercising every combination forces both truth values of the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: CoC subsumes PC. All 2^n rows include at least one true and one false row (for any non-constant predicate), so PC is met.

questiontext.text: Any test set that satisfies Combinatorial Coverage also satisfies Clause Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — every clause is true in some combinations and false in others.
CoC subsumes CC: all 2^n rows make each clause both true and false.

generalfeedback.text: CoC subsumes CC. Across all 2^n combinations each clause takes both values, so CC is met.

name.text: Which criterion needs the most tests

questiontext.text: For a predicate with several independent clauses, which criterion generally demands the largest number of tests?

feedback.text: Correct — CoC requires all 2^n combinations.
PC needs only 2 tests, the fewest.
CC needs as few as 2 tests when clauses are independent.

answer.text: They all need the same number

feedback.text: CoC (2^n) grows far beyond the 2-test minimum of PC and CC.

generalfeedback.text: CoC scales as 2^n and subsumes PC and CC, so it generally requires the most tests.

name.text: PC min vs CoC for 3 clauses

questiontext.text: For a predicate with 3 clauses, Predicate Coverage needs a minimum of 2 tests while Combinatorial Coverage imposes 8 test requirements.

feedback.text: Correct — PC min is 2; CoC is 2^3 = 8.
PC needs only 2 tests, and CoC needs 2^3 = 8, so the statement holds.

generalfeedback.text: PC always needs 2 tests (both predicate values); CoC needs all 2^n = 8 combinations for n = 3.

questiontext.text: Satisfying Clause Coverage always guarantees that Predicate Coverage is also satisfied.

feedback.text: Correct — for a && b, tests {(T,F),(F,T)} meet CC but the predicate is never true.
CC does not subsume PC: a && b with {(T,F),(F,T)} meets CC yet fails PC.

generalfeedback.text: CC and PC are incomparable. The classic counterexample is a && b with {(T,F),(F,T)}: CC met, PC failed.

name.text: Tests to meet both PC and CC (a AND b)

questiontext.text: For p = a && b, what is the minimum number of tests that satisfies both PC and CC?

feedback.text: Correct — {(T,T),(F,F)} makes p both values and each clause both values.
Two tests, (T,T) and (F,F), already meet both criteria.
4 is the full truth table (CoC); PC and CC together need only 2.
One test yields only one predicate value, so PC cannot be met.

generalfeedback.text: The set {(T,T),(F,F)} gives p = true then false (PC) and a, b each both values (CC), so 2 tests suffice.

name.text: Feasible CoC with mutually exclusive clauses

questiontext.text: A predicate uses the clauses x > 0 and x < 0 over a single variable x. Of the 4 combinations Combinatorial Coverage would require, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — both true is impossible; the other three (TF, FT, FF at x=0) are feasible.
x cannot be both > 0 and < 0, so the (T,T) combination is infeasible.
Three combinations are feasible: x>0, x<0, and x=0.
Only (T,T) is impossible; the other three are all reachable.

generalfeedback.text: x > 0 and x < 0 cannot both hold, so (T,T) is infeasible. TF (x>0), FT (x<0), and FF (x=0) remain: 3 feasible.

name.text: Feasible CoC with a dependent clause

questiontext.text: A predicate uses clauses a: x > 5 and b: x > 10. Since b implies a, how many of the 4 CoC combinations are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — (a=F, b=T) is impossible because b implies a.
b true forces a true, so (a=F, b=T) cannot happen.
Three combos are feasible: x>10, 5<x<=10, and x<=5.
Only one combination is infeasible, leaving 3.

generalfeedback.text: b (x>10) implies a (x>5), so (a=F, b=T) is infeasible. TT (x>10), TF (5<x<=10), FF (x<=5) remain: 3.

questiontext.text: For p = a && b && c, which 2-test set satisfies Clause Coverage but not Predicate Coverage? (rows given as (a, b, c))

feedback.text: Correct — each clause takes both values, yet p is false in both rows.
Here p is true then false, so PC is satisfied too.
a and b never become false, so CC is not met.
a never becomes true, so CC fails.

generalfeedback.text: With (T,F,T) and (F,T,F) each of a, b, c takes both values (CC met), but a && b && c is false in both rows, so PC fails.

name.text: Satisfying rows of (a AND b) OR (c AND d)

questiontext.text: Of the 16 truth-table rows, how many make (a && b) || (c && d) true?

feedback.text: Correct — |a&&b| = 4, |c&&d| = 4, overlap = 1, so 4 + 4 - 1 = 7.
You must subtract the 1 overlapping row (all four true) to avoid double counting.
Inclusion-exclusion gives 4 + 4 - 1 = 7, not 6.
Each conjunction alone is true in 4 rows, but together they cover 7.

generalfeedback.text: a && b is true in 4 rows, c && d in 4 rows; they overlap only when all four are true (1 row). 4 + 4 - 1 = 7.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a OR b OR c OR d

questiontext.text: Of the 16 truth-table rows, how many make a || b || c || d true?

feedback.text: Correct — only the all-false row fails.
The all-false row does not satisfy a disjunction.
Exactly one row (all false) fails, leaving 15.
1 would be a conjunction; a 4-way disjunction is true on 15 rows.

generalfeedback.text: A 4-way disjunction is false only on the single all-false row, so 15 of 16 rows satisfy it.

name.text: Satisfying rows of a AND b AND c AND d

questiontext.text: Of the 16 truth-table rows, how many make a && b && c && d true?

feedback.text: Correct — only the all-true row satisfies a 4-way conjunction.
All four clauses must be true simultaneously, which happens in exactly 1 row.
A conjunction is true only when every clause is true: 1 row.
15 is the count for the disjunction, not the conjunction.

generalfeedback.text: A conjunction is true only when every clause is true, so exactly 1 of the 16 rows satisfies it.

questiontext.text: If two clauses of a predicate can never be true at the same time, then full Combinatorial Coverage (all 2^n rows) is infeasible.

feedback.text: Correct — the combination requiring both clauses true can never be executed.
An unreachable combination means at least one of the 2^n rows cannot be produced, so full CoC is infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: CoC demands every one of the 2^n combinations. If one is logically impossible, the complete set cannot be achieved, so full CoC is infeasible (only the feasible rows can be required).

name.text: Feasible CoC combinations with three clauses

questiontext.text: A predicate uses clauses a: x > 0, b: x < 0, and c: y > 0. Of the 8 CoC combinations, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — the 2 combinations with a=T and b=T (over c) are impossible, leaving 6.
a and b cannot both be true, so the 2 rows with a=T, b=T are infeasible.
Only the 2 rows with a=T and b=T are infeasible; 6 remain.
Two rows (a=T, b=T with c either value) are infeasible, not one.

generalfeedback.text: a and b are mutually exclusive, so both a=T, b=T rows (c=T and c=F) are infeasible: 8 - 2 = 6 feasible.

name.text: CoC requirements after one infeasible combination

questiontext.text: A 2-clause predicate has one infeasible combination. How many Combinatorial Coverage test requirements remain?

feedback.text: Correct — 2^2 = 4 minus the 1 infeasible combination.
The infeasible combination is dropped, leaving 3.
Only one combination is removed, so 3 remain.
Removing one of four combinations leaves three, not one.

generalfeedback.text: CoC would need 2^2 = 4 combinations; removing the single infeasible one leaves 3 feasible requirements.

name.text: CC of a 3-clause predicate needs 3 tests

questiontext.text: Clause Coverage of a predicate with 3 independent clauses requires at least 3 tests.

feedback.text: Correct — one all-true and one all-false test cover all three clauses, so 2 tests suffice.
CC needs only 2 tests: all clauses true, then all false, flips every clause.

generalfeedback.text: The number of tests for CC does not grow with clause count when clauses are independent: 2 tests (all-true, all-false) always suffice.

questiontext.text: For p = a || b, which 2-test set satisfies Clause Coverage but not Predicate Coverage? (rows given as (a, b))

feedback.text: Correct — each clause takes both values, but p is true in both rows, so PC fails.
Here p is true then false, so PC is satisfied.
b never becomes true, so CC is not met (and p is true then false).
p is false then true here, so PC is satisfied.

generalfeedback.text: With (T,F) and (F,T) each clause takes both values (CC met), but a || b is true in both rows, so the predicate is never false and PC fails.

name.text: Satisfying rows of (a OR b) AND (c OR d)

questiontext.text: Of the 16 truth-table rows, how many make (a || b) && (c || d) true?

feedback.text: Correct — (a || b) holds in 3 of 4 (a,b) combos and (c || d) in 3 of 4 (c,d) combos: 3 x 3 = 9.
Each disjunction holds in 3 of its 4 combos, so 3 x 3 = 9, not 12.
7 is the count for (a && b) || (c && d), a different predicate.
Multiply the independent halves: 3 x 3 = 9.

generalfeedback.text: The two halves are over disjoint clauses. a || b is true in 3 of 4 (a,b) rows; c || d in 3 of 4 (c,d) rows. 3 x 3 = 9.

name.text: Tests to meet both PC and CC (a OR b OR c)

questiontext.text: For p = a || b || c, what is the minimum number of tests that satisfies both PC and CC?

feedback.text: Correct — {(T,T,T),(F,F,F)} makes p both values and each clause both values.
Two tests, all-true and all-false, already meet both criteria.
8 is the CoC size; PC and CC together need only 2.
Two well-chosen tests suffice for PC and CC together.

generalfeedback.text: {(T,T,T),(F,F,F)} gives p = true then false (PC) and each clause both values (CC), so 2 tests suffice.

name.text: PC infeasible for a contradictory predicate

questiontext.text: For p = a && !a, Predicate Coverage is infeasible because the predicate can never be true.

feedback.text: Correct — a and !a are contradictory, so p is always false and can never be made true.
a && !a is a contradiction; the predicate is false for every input, so PC (which needs a true case) is infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: The clauses a and !a are dependent (one is the negation of the other), so a && !a is always false. PC requires a true evaluation, which is impossible here.

name.text: Satisfying rows of NOT (a OR b) AND (c OR d)

questiontext.text: Of the 16 truth-table rows, how many make !(a || b) && (c || d) true?

feedback.text: Correct — !(a || b) forces a=F, b=F (1 combo), and (c || d) holds in 3 of 4: 1 x 3 = 3.
!(a || b) is true in only 1 of the 4 (a,b) combos, not 3; the answer is 1 x 3 = 3.
a=F, b=F is required, so only 3 of the (c || d) rows qualify.
c || d contributes 3 rows, not 1, once a=F and b=F are fixed.

generalfeedback.text: !(a || b) is true only when a=F and b=F (1 of 4 combos); c || d is true in 3 of 4. Total = 1 x 3 = 3.
